n: David praises the Lord for drawing him up, like water lifted from a well, so his enemies had no reason to celebrate. The heading calls it a song for the dedication of the house.

f.g: The Hebrew pictures drawing up a bucket from a well.

n: A short, simple testimony: I cried, and you healed me. Healing may be physical, emotional, or spiritual.
David had been near death, almost in the grave, but God brought him back. Being rescued from the pit is a preview of resurrection hope.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the realm of the dead.

n: David invites the faithful to join him in thanks. Personal deliverance becomes a reason for the whole community to praise.

f.g: Hebrew ḥasidim — the faithful, loyal ones who keep covenant.

n: One of the most comforting verses in scripture: God’s discipline is brief, but his favor lasts a lifetime. Sorrow may stay overnight like a guest, but joy arrives with the morning.
David confesses that when things were going well, he grew self-confident and thought nothing could shake him.
He realizes his strength had been God’s gift all along. When God hid his face, David was immediately shaken.

f.g: An image of a secure position or stronghold — possibly his kingdom.
To withdraw his presence and favor.

n: In his trouble David returned to prayer, pleading for mercy.

David reasons with God: what good would my death do you? The dead can’t sing praise. Ancient Israel’s hope beyond the grave was still developing; later revelation teaches that the dead hear the gospel.
A short, honest cry: hear me, have mercy, help me.
God turned grief into celebration. Sackcloth was rough mourning clothing; God took it off and dressed David in joy instead.

f.g: Coarse goat-hair cloth worn in mourning or repentance.

n: The purpose of deliverance is praise. David vows his whole being will sing and give thanks forever.

f.g: Often understood as “my soul” or “my whole self.”
